blocks.eyebrow: HUGHES ROOM VIEWS · THE LIVING WORLD
blocks.title:
The hidden
world of fungi.
blocks.intro: A mushroom is only part of the story. Step into a world of tiny spores, secret threads, and surprising science.

entry.note: Two exhibits to explore. Our classroom discoveries are coming next.

blocks.title: Small. Strange. Extraordinary.
blocks.intro: Fungi have a kingdom of their own. Here are three examples, shown at different zoom levels.

cards.title: Mushroom makers
cards.body: Some fungi grow mushrooms. A mushroom is the part that makes and releases spores.

media.alt: A group of small blue Mycena interrupta mushrooms growing among moss and wood.
media.caption: Real blue mushrooms growing on wood. Can you find the smallest cap?

cards.title: Fuzzy molds
cards.body: Many molds grow as tiny branching threads. That fuzz is a fungus growing.

media.alt: Fine pale Rhizopus mold threads on a strawberry, topped by tiny dark round spore cases.
media.caption: The tiny dark dots are cases that hold spores.

cards.title: Tiny yeasts
cards.body: Yeasts are fungi too. They usually live as single cells, too small to see on their own.

media.alt: Oval Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast cells seen with a microscope; several have small buds.
media.caption: A microscope shows these yeast cells. Some have a tiny bud growing from them.

learning.action: Choose a photograph to look closer.
learning.observe: What can you see in one picture that you cannot see in another?
learning.teacher: These are examples of fungal forms, not three separate scientific groups. A single fungus can have more than one growth form.

words.body: A large group scientists use to organize living things.

station.title: Fungi up close
station.intro: Meet real fungi. Peek under a cap. Follow the hidden threads.

blocks.title: There’s more under that cap.
blocks.intro: Choose a number to find a part. This model shows a mushroom with gills. Other mushrooms can look different.

hotspots.label: Cap
hotspots.body: The cap holds the spore-making surface underneath it. Look below the umbrella!

hotspots.label: Gills
hotspots.body: These thin plates under the cap make spores. Not all mushrooms have gills.

hotspots.label: Stem
hotspots.body: The stem lifts the cap. This helps spores reach moving air.

hotspots.label: Mycelium
hotspots.body: A network of tiny branching threads is called mycelium. These threads are part of the fungus.

hotspots.label: Spores
hotspots.body: A spore can start new fungal growth in the right conditions. The spores in this model are enlarged.

detailMedia.alt: A real close-up of the thin ridges under a mushroom cap, radiating out from its stem.
detailMedia.caption: A real example of gills: the ridges under a mushroom cap. This photograph stays the same as you explore the model.

learning.observe: Which part makes spores? Which part is a network of threads?
learning.teacher: This is one model of a gilled mushroom. It is not a mushroom identification guide.

words.body: A network of tiny branching threads that is part of a fungus.
One fungal thread is a hypha. More than one are hyphae.
A tiny structure that can start new fungal growth in the right conditions.

blocks.title: The mushroom is just the beginning.
blocks.intro: A mushroom is only part of this fungus. What else could be growing inside the wood or soil?

media.alt: White cottony mycelium spreading in a branching patch over a piece of wood.
media.caption: Real mycelium on wood. Can you find where the fine threads spread out?

views.label: Above the surface
views.body: The mushroom makes and releases spores. Much of this fungus can be hidden from view.

views.label: Below the surface
views.body: Mycelium is a network of tiny threads. It can spread through soil or wood and take in food.

learning.action: Switch views, then grow the threads.
learning.observe: Where do new branches begin? Follow them back to a mushroom.
learning.teacher: The fruiting body and mycelium are connected parts of a fungus. The highlighted threads are enlarged and growth is greatly sped up.

words.body: The spore-making part of a fungus. A mushroom is one kind.

blocks.title: A tiny drop. An incredible launch.
blocks.intro: Compare the model with a real microscope recording. Then follow the spores into the breeze.

steps.title: A spore lands
steps.body: In a suitable place, a spore can start growing a tiny thread.

steps.title: Threads spread
steps.body: Tiny threads grow and branch into a network. That network is mycelium.

steps.title: A mushroom grows
steps.body: With suitable conditions, the fungus may grow a mushroom. Not every spore gets this far!

steps.title: Spores set off
steps.body: A gilled mushroom releases spores from its gills. Once clear of the cap, they can drift on air currents.

video.title: Through a microscope
video.caption: Watch the round spore jump from right to left. Scientists filmed this through a microscope and slowed it down.

plumeVideo.title: A puffball sends out a cloud
plumeVideo.caption: Watch the cloud of spores! In this research recording, a scientist squeezes a dried puffball. Its spores leave through a small opening. Puffballs release spores differently from gilled mushrooms. The video is slowed five times.

words.body: Tiny structures that can start new fungal growth in suitable conditions.

station.title: Life in motion
station.intro: Choose an investigation. Follow spores, discover living light, or turn a pattern into music.

activities.label: Tiny launch
activities.title: A tiny drop. An incredible launch.
activities.intro: How can a water drop help a spore leave a gill? Compare the model with a real microscope recording.

learning.action: Launch the model, then play the microscope video.
learning.observe: What joins just before the spore moves?
learning.teacher: Many gilled fungi use this surface-tension mechanism. The model enlarges and slows it; the recording is a real microscope view.

activities.label: Ride the breeze
activities.title: Where can the breeze take a spore?
activities.intro: Once a spore falls clear of a cap, moving air can carry it away. Try changing the breeze in this model.

learning.action: Release spores, then change the breeze.
learning.observe: What changes when the breeze goes the other way?
learning.teacher: This model shows transport after release. It does not show the water-drop launch through a microscope. Spores are enlarged; speed and distances are illustrative.

activities.label: Spore cloud
activities.title: A puffball sends out a cloud.
activities.intro: Puffballs hold spores inside. Many tiny spores together make the cloud you see in this research video.

learning.observe: Where does the cloud leave the puffball?
learning.safety: Watch only. Do not squeeze wild mushrooms or breathe in a spore cloud.
learning.teacher: A scientist compresses a dried puffball in a research demonstration. This differs from discharge by a gilled mushroom. Playback is slowed five times; capture frame rate is not supplied.

activities.label: Life cycle
activities.title: From a spore to more spores.
activities.intro: Explore four stages of a mushroom-making fungus. A spore needs suitable conditions to grow. Many never grow into mushrooms.

learning.observe: Where could the story start again?
learning.teacher: This is a simplified cycle. For many mushroom-forming fungi, compatible threads must join before a mushroom can form.

blocks.title: Fungi have many jobs.
blocks.intro: Some fungi recycle dead leaves and wood. Some partner with plants. Others help us make bread.

cards.title: The recyclers
cards.body: Some fungi break down dead wood and leaves. Nutrients return to the environment and can be used again.

learning.action: Follow the recycling, one step at a time.
learning.observe: What happens before the fungus takes in food?
learning.teacher: Fungi release enzymes outside their threads. These break down complex material into smaller molecules that can be absorbed. Nutrients are recycled through decomposition.

cards.title: The plant partners
cards.body: Some fungi partner with plant roots. The plant gives sugar. The fungus helps the plant get water and minerals.

learning.action: Choose a direction to follow the trade.
learning.observe: What goes to the fungus? What goes to the plant?
learning.teacher: Plants make sugars using light. This partnership occurs in some plant–fungus relationships; it does not describe all fungi.

cards.title: The tiny bakers
cards.body: Baker’s yeast makes gas as it feeds on sugars. Little gas bubbles help bread dough rise.

learning.observe: What happens to the dough as the gas pockets grow?
learning.teacher: The gas is carbon dioxide. This is a sped-up model of fermentation, with enlarged gas pockets, not yeast cells.

learning.observe: How does this fungus get food? What changes around it?

words.body: Substances living things need to grow and do their work.

blocks.title: Light. Electricity. A little mystery.
blocks.intro: Some fungi make light. People can also turn measurements from fungi into sound. Those are two different things.

experiments.title: A living night-light
experiments.body: Some fungi make light through a chemical reaction. This is called bioluminescence. Most fungi do not glow.

media.alt: Panellus stipticus mushrooms emitting a green glow in the dark in a long-exposure photograph.
media.caption: Real glowing fungi: Panellus stipticus. The camera collected light for over eight minutes to make the glow easier to see.

experiments.label: Glowing fungi

learning.action: Look closely at the real photograph.
learning.observe: Where can you see light? What does the camera help us see?
learning.teacher: Bioluminescence is light from a chemical reaction. This long exposure makes a faint glow more visible; most fungi do not glow.

experiments.title: Can we hear a pattern?
experiments.body: Scientists have measured electrical changes in fungi. What those changes do is still being studied. A change on a graph is not proof of a message.
experiments.label: Mushroom music

learning.observe: What happens to the notes when the line is higher?
learning.teacher: This activity uses invented data to show a sound-mapping rule. It is not a recording of mushroom measurements. Measurements require careful control of sensor and environmental effects.

words.body: Turning information into sound using a rule chosen by a person.

blocks.title: Think like a scientist.
blocks.intro: Look for clues. Use what you noticed in the exhibits to explain your choices.

cards.title: A ring with a reason
cards.body: Some mycelium grows outward in a circle. Mushrooms appearing around its edge can make a “fairy ring”.

cards.title: A tiny launch
cards.body: Many gilled mushrooms use a tiny drop of liquid to help launch each spore away from a gill.

cards.title: An unexpected relative
cards.body: Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. They still have their very own kingdom!

choices.label: The plant kingdom
choices.feedback: A good question to investigate! Fungi have their own kingdom.

choices.label: A kingdom of their own
choices.feedback: You found it! Fungi belong to their own kingdom.

choices.label: A plant’s roots
choices.feedback: It can look root-like, but mycelium is part of a fungus.

choices.label: A network of fungal threads
choices.feedback: Exactly! One thread is a hypha. A network of them is mycelium.

questions.prompt: You spot a mushroom outdoors. What should you do?

choices.label: Use its color to decide if I can taste it
choices.feedback: Pictures and colors cannot tell us a mushroom is safe. Leave it where it is and ask an adult.

choices.label: Look without tasting, and tell an adult
choices.feedback: That is careful exploring. Never taste a wild mushroom.

learning.action: Choose an answer, then read the clue.
learning.observe: Which exhibit helps explain your answer?
learning.safety: Look closely outdoors, but never taste a wild mushroom. Pictures and colors cannot tell us it is safe to eat. Leave moldy food to an adult.

blocks.title: Now it’s our turn to wonder.
blocks.intro: Our classroom photographs, observations, and discoveries will appear here when our journal is ready.
